flashcards.q: Why is LIKE '%word%' slow on a big table?
flashcards.a: The leading % makes the B-tree index unusable, so every row has to be read and compared (a full table scan).
flashcards.more: A B-tree index is sorted by the first letters of the text, like a dictionary. `LIKE 'phone%'` can follow the index, but in `LIKE '%phone%'` even the starting point is unknown. With ten times the data, it takes ten times as long. On top of that, LIKE ignores typos and has no idea which result fits best.

flashcards.q: What is an inverted index?
flashcards.a: A list that records, for every word, which documents contain it.
flashcards.more: It works like the index at the back of a book: "pasta: pages 12, 87". To search, you never read a document; you just fetch the word's list (its posting list). For several words, the lists are combined. That is why search stays at milliseconds even on tens of millions of documents.

flashcards.q: What are the three parts of an analyzer?
flashcards.a: A character filter (cleanup), a tokenizer (cuts into words) and token filters (lowercase, stop words, stemming).
flashcards.more: An analyzer turns text into terms that are ready for the index. "Samsung Phones" becomes samsung and phone. So whether someone searches "phone" or "PHONES", it matches. You can see how any text is split with the `_analyze` API.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if indexing and searching use different analyzers?
flashcards.a: The terms on the two sides differ, so a word that is in the index never matches the search.
flashcards.more: A search engine doesn't understand meaning; it matches terms exactly. If the index holds "phone" and the query produces "Phones", there is no match. Hence the rule: the same analyzer on both sides. In Elasticsearch, once you set the analyzer on a field, queries on that field use it automatically.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between text and keyword fields in Elasticsearch?
flashcards.a: text runs an analyzer, for full-text search. keyword is one exact value, for filters, sorting and facets.
flashcards.more: A product name or description is text, because customers search by any word inside it. Brand, status and category are keyword, because they are matched or counted as a whole. Running an aggregation on a text field makes Elasticsearch return an error.

flashcards.q: Which three things does BM25 look at to score a document?
flashcards.a: How rare the word is across the index, how often it appears in the document, and how short the text is.
flashcards.more: A rare word carries more information, so matching it scores higher. Repetition raises the score too, but flattens out after a point. A match in short text is worth more than a match in the corner of a long one. On top of this, a boost can give a field such as the name extra weight.

flashcards.q: What is a facet?
flashcards.a: A counted list that splits the results into groups, such as Samsung (12), Apple (8).
flashcards.more: Facets show customers what is in the results and let them narrow the list with one click. In Elasticsearch you build them with an aggregation, and the field must be a keyword. The search results and the facets come back in the same request.

flashcards.q: In a bool query, what is the difference between must and filter?
flashcards.a: must conditions calculate a score; filter only answers yes or no, leaves the score alone and is cached.
flashcards.more: The customer's search words go in must, because "how well does it fit" matters there. Brand, a price range or in-stock status go in filter. Putting everything in must still works, but the query is slower and the scores change for no reason.

flashcards.q: What is post_filter for in a faceted search?
flashcards.a: It trims the hits after the aggregation has counted, so the facet still shows every brand even after the customer picks one.
flashcards.more: A brand condition inside the main query shrinks the counts too, so the facet would show only Samsung (12). In post_filter, the counts are made first and the hits are trimmed afterwards. The price: post_filter isn't cached and speeds nothing up, so use it only for the facet's own field and keep other conditions in filter.

flashcards.q: How does database full-text search work in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.a: A tsvector column holds the terms, a GIN index (an inverted index) makes it fast, and @@ matches it against a tsquery.
flashcards.more: A generated column keeps the terms in step with the row, so there is no sync job. `ts_rank` orders the results. What you give up: typo tolerance (add the pg_trgm extension for some), facets and BM25-grade ranking. For a few thousand to a few hundred thousand rows it is often all you need.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't the search index be the only home of your real data?
flashcards.a: It is a copy: it lags by a second or two, has no transactions, and a mapping change means rebuilding it all.
flashcards.more: The source of truth lives in the database. Design on the assumption that you can delete the search index any day and rebuild it from the database. Take decisions about price or stock from the database. How to keep the copy fresh: [[caching/search-pipeline/dual-write-drift|keeping the search index up to date]].

flashcards.q: What is the dual write problem?
flashcards.a: Writing the same data to two separate systems independently; if one succeeds and the other fails, they disagree.
flashcards.more: For example, a controller flushes to the database and then writes straight to Elasticsearch. If the second write fails, the product is in the database but not in search, and nobody retries. You can't write "all or nothing" across two systems, so you treat one as the original and run the other behind it through a queue.

flashcards.q: Which is the source of truth, the search index or the database?
flashcards.a: The database. The search index is its copy, and can be deleted and rebuilt on any day.
flashcards.more: Every write goes to the database first, and the index follows behind it. So decisions about price, stock or permissions always check the database. Losing the index costs you time; losing the database costs you the business.

flashcards.q: Why does an indexing message carry only the ID, not the full data?
flashcards.a: The worker then reads the latest state from the database, so the index never gets old data even if a message arrives twice or out of order.
flashcards.more: If the message carried the price, two price-change messages arriving out of order would leave the old price in the index. With just an ID, the message means "look at this product again", and the result is correct whenever you run it. The messages stay small too.

flashcards.q: What is the simple way to make an index handler idempotent?
flashcards.a: Use the product ID as the document ID and PUT the whole document.
flashcards.more: Idempotent means doing it once or many times gives the same result. A queue sometimes delivers a message twice, so without this property the same product would show up twice in search. A POST without an ID does exactly that: it creates a new document every time.

flashcards.q: What happens to indexing messages while Elasticsearch is down?
flashcards.a: The handler throws, Messenger retries with growing delays, and if every try fails the message is parked in the failed transport.
flashcards.more: The database write still succeeds and customers notice nothing. Only search stays stale for a while. With the retry settings shown, the retries cover about 4 minutes. A longer outage parks the messages in the failed transport, and `messenger:failed:retry` runs them again once Elasticsearch is back.

flashcards.q: What can still go wrong between flush() and dispatch(), and how do you cover it?
flashcards.a: The process can die between them: the product is saved but no message exists. Cover it with a nightly re-send job, or the outbox pattern.
flashcards.more: The nightly job re-sends IndexProduct for every product changed in the last 24 hours. It is safe because the handler is idempotent, but a lost message can wait up to a day. The outbox writes the message in the same transaction as the product, so it can't be lost, at the cost of an extra table and a relay.

flashcards.q: What does eventual consistency mean for search?
flashcards.a: After a database write, the index runs a second or two behind, then catches up on its own.
flashcards.more: The gap comes from queue waiting, the worker's work and Elasticsearch's refresh interval (usually 1 second). It isn't a bug but the normal price of this design. When load rises, the gap grows, so measure the number and age of the messages waiting in the queue.

flashcards.q: Where should the page a user sees right after writing something read its data from?
flashcards.a: From the database, not from the search index.
flashcards.more: The index runs behind, so reading from it means users can't find what they just wrote and think the save failed. Let the "My products" list, the edit page and order details come from the database. Keep search only for finding other people's things.

flashcards.q: What is an alias in Elasticsearch, and why does the app always use one?
flashcards.a: An alias is a nickname for an index. It can be flipped to a new index in one atomic step, so a reindex needs no code change and no downtime.
flashcards.more: The app only knows `products`; whether that means products_v1 or products_v2 is decided by the alias. You flip it after the new index is completely filled and verified. If you keep the old index for a few days, a rollback is just flipping the alias back.

flashcards.q: When do you have to rebuild the whole search index?
flashcards.a: When an analyzer or a field type changes, when drift from the database has built up, or when the index is lost.
flashcards.more: You can't change the analyzer or type of an existing field, because the old documents are already stored as terms under the old rules. So you build a new index with the new mapping and fill it from the database in batches (`_bulk`). Being able to do this at any time is the proof that the index really is a copy.

flashcards.q: What are a cache hit and a cache miss?
flashcards.a: Hit: the answer was found in the cache. Miss: it wasn't there, so it had to be fetched from the real source (the database).
flashcards.more: The higher the hit rate, the more useful the cache. The first request for something is always a miss; after that miss the answer sits in the cache, and the following requests get hits.

flashcards.q: A page opens 50,000 times a day and its query takes 800ms. What does caching save?
flashcards.a: About 11 hours of database work a day. With a 10-minute cache the query runs at most 144 times, under 2 minutes.
flashcards.more: 50,000 x 800ms is 40,000 seconds. Cached for 10 minutes, the query runs at most 6 times an hour, 144 times a day, about 115 seconds in total. And each visitor waits about 3ms instead of 800ms.

flashcards.q: How does the cache-aside strategy work?
flashcards.a: The app looks in the cache first; if it isn't there, the app fetches it from the database itself and stores it in the cache.
flashcards.more: The cache fetches nothing; looking up, fetching and filling all happen in the app's code. That is why the app keeps working when the cache is down, only slower. It is also called lazy loading, because the cache is filled only when something is asked for.

flashcards.q: What happens to a cache-aside app when the cache goes down at peak traffic?
flashcards.a: Every request becomes a miss and goes to the database. The app stays correct, but a busy site's database may fall over.
flashcards.more: The app keeps working because the truth lives in the database. But the database was counting on the cache to absorb most reads. A small site survives the extra load; a busy one may not, so keep an eye on the cache and make sure the database can cope with a cold cache, at least briefly.

flashcards.q: What does Symfony's CacheInterface::get($key, $callback) do?
flashcards.a: If the key exists it returns the stored value; if not, it runs the callback, stores the result and returns it.
flashcards.more: Inside the callback you set the expiry with `$item->expiresAfter(600)`. This is Symfony's form of cache-aside. The three steps "look up, build if missing, store" happen in one call, and you don't write a separate if.

flashcards.q: How does a write travel in write-through?
flashcards.a: To both the cache and the database at once; it counts as done only when both finish.
flashcards.more: As a result the cache is almost never stale. The price: every write is slower, because it waits for two places. And caching data that nobody will read later wastes space for nothing.

flashcards.q: What is the biggest risk of write-behind?
flashcards.a: Writes go to the cache first and the database later. If the cache dies before they reach the database, they are lost.
flashcards.more: You gain speed because the user doesn't wait for the database. But for money, orders or permissions you can't leave room for loss. So it is used only for load-absorbing writes where losing a little doesn't matter.

flashcards.q: What must the key contain when you cache an answer that differs per user?
flashcards.a: The user's ID or identity. Otherwise one person's data is seen by another.
flashcards.more: For example `cart.user.42`, not `cart`. This isn't just a caching mistake but a security one: private data leaks. When in doubt, don't cache personal data, or give it a short expiry.

flashcards.q: What kind of data is better left uncached?
flashcards.a: Account balances, checkout stock, and anything cheap to build or never asked for twice.
flashcards.more: Caching means buying speed with the risk of staleness. For data where a wrong value causes direct loss, that trade doesn't pay. And for data that is cheap to build, the cache's complexity outweighs the gain.

flashcards.q: What is cache invalidation?
flashcards.a: Deleting or voiding the cache's old copy when the real data changes.
flashcards.more: A cache is a copy of the real data, so when the original changes, the copy doesn't change by itself. Without invalidation, users see stale data. It is so hard that people joke there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.

flashcards.q: What is a TTL, and why should every cache entry have one?
flashcards.a: A TTL is an entry's lifetime; when it ends, the entry disappears. Even if you forget to invalidate, the mistake lasts only until expiry.
flashcards.more: A TTL is a safety net. If somewhere in the code an invalidation is missed, then without a TTL the stale data would stay forever. The question for setting a TTL: "What is the longest this data can be out of date?"

flashcards.q: What TTL should important data like prices get?
flashcards.a: A short one, such as 1 minute, plus direct invalidation the moment the price changes.
flashcards.more: A long TTL leaves the wrong price visible for a long time, while a short TTL on its own isn't a guarantee. So use two layers: delete on change (the main mechanism) and a short TTL (the last line of defense).

flashcards.q: What must a cache key contain?
flashcards.a: Everything that changes the answer: ID, user, language, page, sort, and a shape version.
flashcards.more: If a `products` key has no page or language, asking for page 2 can return page 1. If per-user data has no user in the key, information leaks. Example: `products.v2.cat7.page2.sort-price.en`.

flashcards.q: What is a versioned cache key good for?
flashcards.a: When the shape inside the cache changes, bumping the key version (v1 to v2) voids every old entry at once.
flashcards.more: The new code looks up v2 keys, so nobody reads the v1 entries and they die at their TTL. You never delete them one by one. During a deploy that changes the shape this is nearly essential, otherwise new code that finds old-shaped entries can break.

flashcards.q: What does bumping a cache key version cost you?
flashcards.a: The new keys start empty, so the first requests all miss and hit the database together.
flashcards.more: Old entries are never read again, so there is nothing to delete, but nothing is warm either. For a hot key such as the homepage list, many requests miss at once. Protect it with jitter, a lock or stale-while-revalidate (see the stampede lesson). For a rarely read key it hardly matters.

flashcards.q: What is a cache tag good for in Symfony?
flashcards.a: Tag several entries with one tag and a single invalidateTags() call deletes them all.
flashcards.more: Use `TagAwareCacheInterface` and call `$item->tag(['product_42'])` in the callback. When the product changes, call `invalidateTags(['product_42'])`. You don't have to remember which entries contain the product. With Redis, use `cache.adapter.redis_tag_aware`.

flashcards.q: How can a category list be cleared when one of its products changes?
flashcards.a: Tag the list with the id of every product inside it. Then invalidateTags(['product_42']) removes the product page and the list together.
flashcards.more: Without that tag on the list, only the product's own entry goes and the list keeps showing the old price. The price: a list of 500 products carries 500 tags, so do this for short lists, such as one page of 20. The list is rebuilt on its next read.

flashcards.q: When a database change must also clear the cache, what is the right order?
flashcards.a: Write to the database and commit first, then delete from the cache.
flashcards.more: Delete first and, in the gap, another request can read the old value and put it back in the cache, where nobody deletes it again. Delete after the commit and the next miss fetches the new value. A tiny gap still remains, so keep a TTL too.

flashcards.q: What is a cache stampede?
flashcards.a: When a popular entry expires, many requests miss at once and send the same heavy query to the database.
flashcards.more: Each request gets its own miss, and none knows the others are doing the same job. The database suddenly takes a thousand times the load. The cache had been keeping the database alive, so when the cache fails, the database falls over too.

flashcards.q: A key takes 800ms to rebuild and 1,000 requests miss together. How much work is that?
flashcards.a: About 800 seconds of query work arriving in one second, far more than the database can do, so everything slows down.
flashcards.more: Each query is normal on its own; a thousand identical ones at the same moment are not. The fix is to turn them into one query (a lock) or to stop the entries dying together (jitter).

flashcards.q: Are a thundering herd and a cache stampede different?
flashcards.a: Nearly the same thing: many processes waking up and pouncing on one resource together. In the cache context it is called a stampede.
flashcards.more: "Thundering herd" is a broader term: everyone waking at once when a lock is released, or all clients retrying together when a server comes back. In caching, its form is the stampede (dogpile).

flashcards.q: How does a lock stop a stampede?
flashcards.a: For one key, only one request takes the lock and builds the new value; the rest wait or take the stale value.
flashcards.more: So one heavy query runs instead of 1,000. This is also called request coalescing. Whoever didn't get the lock has two paths: wait briefly and check the cache again, or show the old value immediately.

flashcards.q: What is jitter, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Adding a random few seconds to a TTL so many entries don't die together.
flashcards.more: If many entries filled at the same moment get the same TTL, they die at the same moment. With `expiresAfter(600 + random_int(0, 120))` the expiry is spread out. It costs almost nothing, so it is good to add every time.

flashcards.q: How does probabilistic early expiration work?
flashcards.a: Before the expiry, with a higher probability the closer it gets, some request rebuilds the value ahead of time.
flashcards.more: Symfony Cache's `get($key, $callback, beta: 1.0)` does this by itself. Raising beta starts the attempts earlier. beta: 0 turns it off, and `\INF` rebuilds right now.

flashcards.q: What is stale-while-revalidate?
flashcards.a: Serving the old value immediately even after it has expired, while one request builds the new value behind the scenes.
flashcards.more: The entry has two times: soft (after which it should be rebuilt) and hard (after which it is deleted). After the soft time, one request takes a lock and rebuilds, and the rest get the old value. The user never waits; the price is a slightly old value for a while.

flashcards.q: Why does a cache-rebuild lock need a TTL and try/finally?
flashcards.a: Otherwise, if the lock holder crashes, the lock hangs forever and every other request gets stuck and uses up the PHP workers.
flashcards.more: A short lock TTL (say 30 seconds) guarantees the lock frees itself even if the holder dies. Calling release() in finally frees the lock even when an exception is thrown. For the waiters, always keep a fallback: the stale value or a short wait.

flashcards.q: Why do we need HTTP caching?
flashcards.a: To use a copy in the browser or CDN instead of fetching the same file or answer from the server again and again, so pages open faster and server costs fall.
flashcards.more: A request that never reaches the server is the fastest one. The server then builds only what has actually changed. Bandwidth drops too, and that lands directly on a CDN or cloud bill.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between Cache-Control: no-cache and no-store?
flashcards.a: no-cache: a copy may be kept, but you must ask the server before using it. no-store: no copy may be kept anywhere.
flashcards.more: The name makes no-cache widely misunderstood. For sensitive answers (tokens, bank details) use no-store. For HTML pages, no-cache usually works: the browser validates with an ETag and gets a 304 if nothing changed.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a public and a private cache?
flashcards.a: private: only the user's own browser may keep it. public: a CDN or proxy may keep it too.
flashcards.more: Personal answers, such as a dashboard or profile, must be private. A public cache hands everyone the same copy, so it is safe only for answers that are identical for everybody. `s-maxage` applies only to shared caches.

flashcards.q: How do ETag and If-None-Match work?
flashcards.a: The server sends an ETag with the answer. The browser later sends it back in If-None-Match; if it matches, the server replies 304 with no body.
flashcards.more: 304 Not Modified means "your copy is right, nothing new". No body is downloaded, which saves the download. The request still goes to the server, so to save that cost you need max-age.

flashcards.q: What does stale-while-revalidate=60 do?
flashcards.a: After expiry, the old copy may still be shown for 60 seconds, while the cache fetches a new one behind the scenes.
flashcards.more: The user doesn't wait, because the old copy comes back immediately. The next request gets the new copy. The same idea works in a cache inside your server; the price is slightly old data for a short time.

flashcards.q: What is cache busting?
flashcards.a: Putting a hash of a file's contents in its name (app-3f9a1c.js), so that a change gives it a new name and the old cache is bypassed.
flashcards.more: A new hashed file name is a new URL, which means a new cache key. That makes it safe to give the file a one-year `immutable` lifetime. HTML pages must stay on a short lifetime, because the links to the new names live in the HTML.

flashcards.q: Why is a one-year max-age on /assets/app.js dangerous if the file name never changes?
flashcards.a: Browsers keep the old copy as fresh for a year and never ask again, so users keep running the old file after a deploy. Put a content hash in the name.
flashcards.more: The URL is the cache key: a fixed name means the browser sees nothing new. With a hashed name, each deploy is a new URL, so the long lifetime is safe. The price is that the HTML must stay short-lived, and files that need a fixed URL (robots.txt) get a short max-age plus an ETag instead.

flashcards.q: What decides the cache key in a CDN?
flashcards.a: Usually the URL (query string included), plus the request headers named in the Vary header (such as Accept-Language).
flashcards.more: If the same URL gives different answers (language, device), you need Vary, or the wrong copy gets served. But with `Vary: Cookie`, every user gets their own key and hits drop to zero. So use Vary sparingly.

flashcards.q: Which answers are dangerous to mark Cache-Control: public?
flashcards.a: Answers that differ by user or cookie, such as a dashboard, a profile or a cart.
flashcards.more: A CDN keeps copies by URL. If the answer depends on the user, the first person's copy reaches the others, and that is a data leak. Give such answers private or no-store.
